motifs: d4 break prepared behind the knight
structures: White's kingside knight temporarily passive on e2
entries.notes: Named for Semyon Alapin; genuinely rare and mild but a real, recognized name a curious student may search for. IMPORTANT DISAMBIGUATION: not the same as the well-known 'Alapin Variation' of the Sicilian Defense (2.c3, ECO B22) — same person's name attached to two unrelated openings, worth flagging to avoid confusion.

motifs: knight repeatedly chased by e5/c4/d4 pawns
structures: White big pawn center vs Black piece pressure from behind
entries.notes: Black invites White to build an imposing pawn center, then attacks it with pieces and timely pawn breaks — the defining hypermodern provocation among the semi-open defenses.

structures: symmetrical-ish center with a slightly weak Black d6 pawn
entries.notes: White trades off the advanced e5 pawn to reach a calmer position with a small, safe structural pull — a common practical choice to sidestep sharp Four Pawns theory, and different enough in character to stand on its own.

structures: four-pawn White center (c4-d4-e5-f4) vs minor-piece pressure
entries.notes: White's most ambitious try, staking out four center pawns; theoretically critical, double-edged, and a large independent body of theory — clearly distinct from the calmer 4.Nf3 main lines.

structures: White e5/d4 center under piece pressure vs solid Black development
entries.notes: The most popular and heavily analyzed modern main line, effectively today's mainstream Alekhine battleground; deserves standalone status alongside the Four Pawns and Exchange tries rather than being folded into the family entry.

Judgment call: kept at historical tier rather than excluded. Named for Adolf Anderssen, who played it occasionally; almost no independent theory exists — it is a genuine flexible/waiting first move that transposes into whatever White chooses next. It has real if thin historical pedigree rather than being a pure joke, which is the distinction from Grob/Bongcloud below.

themes: kingside attack against weakened dark squares
entries.notes: Judgment call: given standalone status rather than folded into Bird's as a branch, because it is a distinct countergambit with its own tactical identity and real club/blitz practice, and because 1...e5 is the single most common way club players punish Bird's Opening — worth its own searchable entry. Tiered historical: real but infrequent above club level, and considered objectively slightly dubious for Black without precise follow-up.

motifs: g4 kingside storm in some lines
entries.notes: Essentially the Dutch Defense with colors reversed and an extra tempo; named for 19th-century English master Henry Bird. Genuine if uncommon practice at club and occasionally titled level; the 'reversed Dutch' resemblance is structural analogy only, not a literal transposition (colors differ).

themes: flexible move order keeping f4/f2-f3 options open
motifs: Qh5/Qf3 quick attacking tries against an unprepared Black
structures: structures typically resolving into Vienna/Italian-like formations
entries.notes: One of the oldest named openings in chess, valued mainly for its move-order flexibility (keeps f4 and Nc3-first options alive) rather than independent structures; the sharp 2...Nf6 3.d4 Urusov Gambit is its best-known named sub-line but is folded into this entry's notes rather than split out, given no lesson yet covers it independently.

Internet-meme opening (popularized in online blitz/bullet play, notably associated with Hikaru Nakamura) that voluntarily forfeits castling rights for no compensation. Included at excluded tier purely for search honesty — a widely-searched name with zero serious instructional content. Not a King's Pawn family entry despite its move order; catalogued here as an irregular/joke opening per scope.

Black's mirror of Grob's Attack (Borg = Grob spelled backwards), a deliberately provocative and objectively weak try associated with Michael Basman. Kept only so search is honest for users who look it up; not a recommended or seriously theoretical line.
Family/root lesson (existing StudySeed) teaches the Classical main line (...dxe4/...Nxe4 Bf5) as its vehicle, with Advance and Exchange shown as branch content.

themes: bishop out before the wall goes up
entries.notes: Covered as branch content inside the existing caro-kann lesson; the direct structural comparison to the French Advance (same chain, free bishop) is the lesson's central point.

entries.fullName: Caro-Kann Defense: Advance Variation, Bayonet Attack
entries.moves: 1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 Bf5 4.Nc3 e6 5.g4 Bg6 6.Nge2 c5
themes: kingside space grab against the bishop
structures: e5/d4 chain, White kingside pawns advanced
entries.notes: Aggressive, committal try against the freshly developed bishop; real modern practice but a single named sideline within the Advance.

themes: doubled pawns for the bishop pair
entries.notes: Judgment call, as flagged in the assignment: a real, named unbalancing try (Bronstein, later Larsen) but a single recapture choice within the 4...Nf6 line rather than a self-sufficient teaching unit — catalogued as a branch.

This is the exact line the existing caro-kann lesson teaches to completion; kept as a distinct catalog entry (planned for its own deeper standalone lesson later) because the ...Bf5 vs. ...Nd7 (Karpov) choice is itself a major theoretical fork worth its own entry.
Direct comparison point to the French Exchange: same pawn skeleton, but Black's light-squared bishop already develops freely, one of the cleanest illustrations of the whole family's central theme.

themes: extra central support at the cost of development
motifs: e4 reinforced by f3, not a piece
entries.notes: Legitimate try (Short, Nunn) that avoids all main-line Caro-Kann theory by supporting e4 with a pawn instead of a piece; genuinely different resulting structures earn it standalone status despite low frequency.

Today's most popular top-level main line, ahead of the immediate ...Bf5 Classical — Black delays the bishop's commitment and keeps more flexibility. Includes the Smyslov sub-choice (...Ngf6, Nxf6+ gxf6) by convention, folded in per the assignment's grouping rather than split into its own entry.

White trades the Exchange Variation's symmetry for an IQP and piece activity; the resulting middlegame is a close structural cousin of IQP positions reached from the Alapin Sicilian and Queen's Gambit Exchange lines (referenced for pedagogical cross-linking, not literal move-transposition).
Move-order device (2.c4 before 3.d4) that reaches the same Panov structure while dodging some early Black tries; not a different middlegame, so kept as a branch note rather than a standalone entry.

themes: flexible piece development before committing pawns
entries.notes: Judgment call: real elite practice (notably Carlsen's world-championship prep) argues for standalone status, but its content is mostly move-order avoidance that transposes into structures covered elsewhere in the family, so it is catalogued as a branch rather than given its own lesson slot. Flagging for orchestrator review.

structures: White typically a tempo behind after the queen is chased
entries.notes: Once a mainstream 19th-century try, now considered too slow at any serious level since ...Nc6 gains a tempo on the exposed queen; kept for real historical/educational value (a clean lesson in why early queen sorties are risky) and as the direct parent of the Danish Gambit (which avoids the tempo loss via 3.c3 instead of 3.Qxd4).

themes: two-pawn sacrifice for a full development lead
structures: White down two pawns for overwhelming piece activity
entries.notes: Sidesteps the Center Game's tempo-loss problem by offering a second pawn instead of grabbing the first back with the queen; a real and still-practiced club-level gambit with an iconic bishop pair on the long diagonals.

Weakens the king's diagonal for no compensation and is considered close to objectively refuted by 3.Nxe5; kept only because the name is a classic 'openings to avoid' reference point beginners plausibly search for.

Bird's Opening (1.f4) is the reversed-color cousin of the Dutch; cross-referenced there, not duplicated here. Family node covering the three major systems (Classical, Stonewall, Leningrad) plus White's Staunton Gambit try.
The historically original Dutch setup (...e6, ...Be7, ...d6, later ...Qe8-h5); less fashionable than Leningrad/Stonewall today but still a fully sound, teachable major line.

entries.moves: 1.d4 f5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Bg2 g6 4.Nf3 Bg7 5.O-O O-O 6.c4 d6
structures: King's-Indian-like fianchetto with an added f5
entries.notes: The modern main-line Dutch (Malaniuk and successors); shares its fianchetto skeleton with the King's Indian Defense but the early f5 changes the tactics enough to stand as its own variation.

entries.moves: 1.d4 f5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Bg2 e6 4.Nf3 d5 5.O-O Bd6 6.c4 c6
motifs: dxc4 exchange to activate the c8-bishop
entries.notes: Structurally the mirror image of White's Stonewall Attack, one file over and with reversed colors — genuinely distinct opening tree, cross-referenced rather than merged. 'Advanced' difficulty: the light-squared bishop's fate is the whole strategic question, and mishandling it is the single most common beginner error in this system.

themes: quick piece activity against a weakened kingside
entries.notes: White's principal specific try against the Dutch; named for Howard Staunton. Modern theory holds accurate Black defense (e.g. ...g6/...Bg7 setups) equalizes, but it remains a real, actively-played anti-Dutch weapon — specialized, not historical.

themes: rapid piece activity for a pawn
entries.notes: Rare and objectively slightly dubious but a real, named countergambit with genuine (if thin) club-level practice; kept historical rather than excluded since it is playable, not a joke.

entries.fullName: English Opening: Botvinnik System (Reversed Closed Sicilian)
entries.moves: 1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nc6 3.g3 g6 4.Bg2 Bg7 5.e4 d6 6.Nge2 Nge7 7.O-O O-O 8.d3 f5
motifs: exchange sac on d5 or c3
entries.notes: Named for Botvinnik's deep, systematic handling (notably vs Portisch, Monte Carlo 1968); a genuine whole-game plan rather than a single move-order trick, which earns it standalone status distinct from the general Reversed Sicilian umbrella.

entries.fullName: English Opening: King's English, Four Knights Variation
entries.notes: Explicitly requested named line; the four-knights piece placement gives it recognizable independent character even though the resulting structures are fluid and often merge into other English/QGD-adjacent middlegames.

entries.moves: 1.c4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nc3 e6 4.g3 b6 5.Bg2 Bb7 6.O-O Be7 7.d4 cxd4 8.Qxd4 d6
entries.notes: A recurring pawn structure (Black pawns on a6/b6/d6/e6) rather than a distinct opening; reached from the Symmetrical English, Sicilian Kan/Taimanov, and Queen's Indian move orders alike. Kept as a structure note under the Symmetrical English rather than a standalone entry.

Existing study id. The family entry stands for 1.c4 broadly and houses Symmetrical English, Reversed Sicilian/King's English, and their subdivisions as children; the existing lesson already teaches both branches at a fundamentals level.

entries.fullName: English Opening: King's English, Reversed Dragon
entries.notes: Recognized subdivision name (mirrors the Sicilian Dragon's g3/Bg2 fianchetto with colors reversed); folded into the Reversed Sicilian umbrella lesson rather than given independent treatment.

entries.moves: 1.c4 e5 2.Nc3 Nf6 3.Nf3 Nc6 4.g3 d5 5.cxd5 Nxd5 6.Bg2 Nb6 7.O-O Be7
entries.notes: Umbrella entry for the King's English subdivisions (Four Knights, Botvinnik/reversed-Closed-Sicilian, Reversed Dragon) under one variation, mirroring how the Sicilian family is organized. 'King's English' is a common alternate name for the whole 1.c4 e5 complex, not a separate subvariation. Its 'reversed Sicilian' character is a structural analogy, not a literal transposition (colors differ), so it is not encoded in transposesTo.

entries.moves: 1.c4 c5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.Nc3 Nc6 4.g3 g6 5.Bg2 Bg7 6.O-O O-O
entries.notes: Standalone-worthy: an enormous body of theory in its own right (double fianchetto, Hedgehog, Rubinstein, Four Knights setups all live here) with a distinct maneuvering character from the Reversed Sicilian half of the English. Hedgehog is treated as a structure note underneath rather than a full standalone entry, since the same structure recurs across several openings.

themes: drawish reputation used as a practical weapon
structures: Scotch Four Knights isolani after d4 exchanges
entries.notes: Historically important solid main line, currently a favored GM drawing weapon (Rubinstein Variation 4.Bb5 Nd4). White's 4th move choice (4.Bb5 Spanish, 4.Bc4 Italian, 4.d4 Scotch) simply transposes into the matching family's structures rather than creating independent theory, so those move-order labels are noted here rather than split into separate entries. No standalone lesson written yet.

entries.fullName: Four Knights Game: Spanish (Ruy Lopez) Variation
entries.notes: Distinguished from plain Ruy Lopez by the extra pair of knights already developed, which enables Black's sharp 4...Nd4 (Rubinstein Variation) — a genuinely independent idea unavailable to the Ruy proper. Kept standalone for that reason.

themes: piece sacrifice for a huge pawn center
structures: massive White pawn center (d4/e4/f4-style expansion) versus Black's extra piece
entries.notes: A genuine sacrifice of a full knight for one pawn, considered objectively dubious with best defense but a real and popular surprise weapon at club and blitz level with an iconic name. Tiered historical rather than excluded because it has real, ongoing amateur practice and a well-worked-out (if unequal) body of theory — not just a joke line. No claim of soundness is made here.
The existing french-defense lesson's main line. Structurally identical chain logic to the Caro-Kann and Tarrasch Advance-type structures.

entries.fullName: French Defense: Advance Variation, Milner-Barry Gambit
entries.moves: 1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.e5 c5 4.c3 Nc6 5.Nf3 Qb6 6.Bd3 cxd4 7.O-O
entries.notes: White declines to recapture on d4 and gambits the pawn for development and attack; real practical history (Spassky) but a club-level sideline of the Advance, not a standalone teaching unit.

entries.moves: 1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7 5.e5 Nfd7 6.Bxe7 Qxe7
themes: piece placement inside a cramped position
entries.notes: Judgment call: Steinitz (4.e5 instead of 4.Bg5) and Burn (4...dxe4) diverge at move 4, so a stricter tree would make them siblings of Classical rather than children; grouped here as branches because standard repertoire literature treats them as members of the Classical complex. Flagging for orchestrator review.

entries.fullName: French Defense: Classical Variation, Burn Variation
entries.notes: Black sidesteps the whole chain-warfare fight by releasing the center early; legitimate but low-frequency at club level, taught as a branch alternative to the main chain lesson.

entries.fullName: French Defense: Classical Variation, Steinitz Variation
entries.moves: 1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e5 Nfd7 5.f4 c5 6.Nf3 Nc6 7.Be3
entries.notes: Same base-strike program as the Advance, taught as a branch since the chain logic is identical; f4 adds a kingside-storm option White lacks in the plain Advance.

Family/root lesson (existing StudySeed) uses the Advance Variation as its main instructional road, with Exchange and a Classical-adjacent (3.Nc3 Nf6 4.e5) line shown as branch content. White frequently sidesteps all French theory with 2.d3/2.Nf3+g3 setups that transpose to the King's Indian Attack (catalog id kings-indian-attack); noted here since the transposition is a defining strategic fact about facing 1...e6, not a separate French variation.

Covered as branch content inside the existing french-defense lesson (3.exd5 exd5 line). Reputation as a drawing weapon is a half-truth: White's Alekhine-style kingside buildup (O-O, Re1, Ne5, Qd3/Bf4) gives real winning chances and merits standalone treatment.

entries.fullName: French Defense: Rubinstein Variation, Fort Knox Variation
themes: trading off the bad bishop early
motifs: early piece trades to a drawish middlegame
entries.notes: Ultra-solid try that solves the French's bad-bishop problem by trading it off before ...e6 even matters; a well-known drawing weapon (Miles, Adams) but too narrow a repertoire choice for standalone treatment.

entries.moves: 1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Bb4 5.e5 h6 6.Bd2 Bxc3 7.bxc3 Ne4
structures: e5/d4 chain with doubled White c-pawns
entries.notes: Named for John Lindsay MacCutcheon (1885); distinct enough from plain Classical to stand alone — Black pins immediately rather than developing with ...Be7, forcing sharp, heavily analyzed lines (including the notorious 7.Ne2/7.Qg4 tries). Spelling 'MacCutcheon' is the standard historical form; 'McCutcheon' is the common alias.

themes: White's extra space vs. Black's simplicity
entries.notes: Low frequency at club level but real, ongoing GM practice (Korchnoi, Bronstein were noted exponents); a solid, low-theory alternative to the Winawer/Classical main roads for a French player who wants a quieter life.
White's most popular modern try specifically because it sidesteps the Winawer pin (3.Nd2 instead of 3.Nc3). The 3...c5 Open Tarrasch is common enough to warrant its own branch entry.

entries.fullName: French Defense: Tarrasch Variation, Open System
entries.notes: Distinct IQP middlegame vs. the Closed Tarrasch's chain structure; taught as a branch rather than standalone since the IQP theme is covered generically elsewhere in the curriculum (Exchange lines, Panov).

entries.moves: 1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e5 c5 5.a3 Bxc3+ 6.bxc3 Ne7
structures: e5/d4 chain with doubled White c-pawns
entries.notes: One of the most theoretically dense and combative lines in all of chess; core rather than merely major given its historical weight (Botvinnik, Korchnoi, Kasparov) and how often serious players must have an answer to it.

entries.fullName: French Defense: Winawer Variation, Poisoned Pawn Variation
entries.moves: 1.e4 e6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.e5 c5 5.a3 Bxc3+ 6.bxc3 Ne7 7.Qg4 Qc7 8.Qxg7 Rg8 9.Qxh7 cxd4
structures: e5/d4 chain with doubled White c-pawns
entries.notes: Famous forcing sideline where Black grabs two pawns while behind in development and races to castle queenside; deep, still-debated theory but a single named sideline, not a standalone teaching unit.

Objectively weak by mainstream engine and master consensus (immediately weakens the kingside dark squares for no compensation), but a genuinely famous named opening (Henry Grob's lifelong advocacy) that users will search for. Kept in the catalog at excluded tier for search honesty rather than given lesson treatment, per scope instruction.

motifs: Bg7 long-diagonal pressure on weak queenside
structures: Benko structure (open a/b-files vs. extra White c-pawn)
entries.notes: Existing lesson. One of the most famous positional pawn sacrifices in chess; long-term queenside pressure fully compensates the pawn in practical play at nearly every level.

structures: Benoni structure (White d5 pawn vs. Black c5/e6)
entries.notes: Umbrella entry for all ...c5 structures against 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 (Modern Benoni, Czech Benoni, Benko Gambit); a genuinely distinct pawn-structure family, hence its own opening-level umbrella beneath the Indian Game family node.

More forcing and less theoretical than Nimzo-Indian since the check typically resolves quickly (trade on d2, or retreat); a practical, lower-maintenance repertoire choice, still important enough to be well known.

themes: quick recapture of the gambit pawn
entries.notes: A real surprise weapon with genuine tactical tricks (see the kieninger-trap study), though a notch below mainstream Indian systems in seriousness of top-level theory; tiered specialized rather than major.

3...Ne4 is a sharper, riskier alternative to the main Budapest recapture (...Ng4); a recognized name but niche enough to stay branch-only rather than a second standalone Budapest entry. No Budapest Gambit lesson exists yet.
3...e5 locks the center immediately instead of recapturing on d5, producing closed King's Indian-like play; legitimate and distinct but a notch below Modern Benoni in popularity.

themes: hypermodern piece pressure vs. pawn center
entries.notes: Black immediately challenges White's center with ...d5 rather than fianchettoing passively; one of the most theoretically rich and combative defenses to 1.d4, core repertoire at every serious level.

themes: big pawn center vs. piece activity
entries.notes: 4.cxd5 Nxd5 5.e4 is the main theoretical battleground of the entire Grünfeld (home to the famous Kasparov-Karpov 'Seville Variation' debates); clearly major standalone material.
A quieter approach avoiding early central tension; real modern practice, lower forcing drama than the Exchange lines but genuinely distinct in character.
5.Qb3 pressures d5 immediately with real independent theory and a distinct strategic character from the Exchange main line.

Umbrella navigation node for every 1.d4 Nf6 system; it is not itself a distinct strategic plan since White's follow-up (or Black's own 2nd move) determines whether the game becomes Nimzo/QI/KID/Grunfeld or something outside this fragment entirely (Trompowsky, London, Torre). Tiered core because recognizing the umbrella and its branch points is foundational knowledge, but whether it deserves its OWN standalone lesson (vs. pure navigation) is a judgment call for the orchestrator — content would overlap heavily with its children.

5.Be2 with an early Bg5 pin; historically significant (Averbakh/Botvinnik era) but lower current top-level frequency than Sämisch, Classical, or Fianchetto — tiered historical rather than specialized.

entries.fullName: King's Indian Defense: Classical Variation (Mar del Plata)
entries.moves: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 g6 3.Nc3 Bg7 4.e4 d6 5.Nf3 O-O 6.Be2 e5 7.O-O Nc6
themes: queenside minority attack vs. kingside storm
entries.notes: The archetypal King's Indian opposite-wing pawn race and the line most people mean by 'King's Indian'; this is the centerpiece the existing kings-indian-defense lesson is built around, so tiered branch-only rather than a competing standalone entry.
Existing lesson. Hypermodern classic: Black concedes the center in exchange for a kingside pawn-storm attack once White locks with d5; among the sharpest, most fighting defenses to 1.d4.
White fianchettoes rather than playing an early e4, producing a quieter, more positional King's Indian fight; a common practical choice against dedicated KID players wanting to sidestep sharp theory.

entries.fullName: King's Indian Defense: Four Pawns Attack
entries.notes: White grabs maximal early space with e4+f4; sharp and somewhat risky for the side playing it, but real and instructive as a test of Black's counterplay resources against an overextended center.
5.f3 produces a structurally distinct King's Indian (no early Nf3, Be3/Qd2 setup, opposite-side attacking races); different enough in plan and structure to justify independent standalone treatment.

themes: queenside space for White vs. piece activity for Black
entries.notes: The sharp, well-known Benoni structure; a real repertoire choice at all levels from club to elite (Kasparov, Topalov associated).

entries.moves: 1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 c5 3.d5 e6 4.Nc3 exd5 5.cxd5 d6 6.e4 g6 7.f4 Bg7 8.Bb5+
entries.notes: 8.Bb5+ is Modern Benoni's sharpest, most theoretically demanding branch (nicknamed the 'Flick-Knife Attack' for White's sudden f4-f5 break); recognized name but no standalone Modern Benoni lesson exists yet to attach branchOfLessonId to.
One of the most respected defenses to 1.d4 at every level; pins Nc3 immediately to fight for e4 and often trades the bishop for structural damage to White's queenside. Foundational core entry.
4.Qc2 sidesteps doubled pawns entirely, producing a different strategic fight from Rubinstein; Capablanca's and later Kasparov's signature weapon. Distinct enough to stand alone.

Keeps White's structural commitments flexible and often transposes into Rubinstein or Queen's Indian lines; real but with less independent significance than the other main systems, so tiered specialized rather than major.
4.Bg5 pins the f6-knight rather than developing normally, leading to real independent tactical theory but at lower frequency than the other four main systems.

By far the most heavily analyzed modern main line (Karpov, Kramnik, Carlsen repertoires); huge body of theory across IQP and hanging-pawn structures. Standalone-worthy tier judgment even without an assigned lesson yet.

4.a3 forces the doubled c-pawns immediately, historically Botvinnik-associated; the most structurally extreme Nimzo-Indian main system, different enough in plan from Rubinstein/Classical to warrant standalone treatment.

Historical precursor to the King's Indian; solid and playable but almost entirely superseded by KID and other systems in modern practice. Real name recognition and genuine historical/educational value keep it in the catalog at historical tier.
Deeply respected, extremely solid system (Karpov and Kramnik repertoire staple) chosen when White avoids 3.Nc3; core alongside Nimzo-Indian as a top-tier defense to 1.d4.

4.a3 forestalls ...Bb4+ pin ideas; a recognized branch but not different enough from mainline Queen's Indian strategy to justify a separate lesson. No standalone Queen's Indian lesson exists yet to attach branchOfLessonId to — left blank pending orchestrator lesson assignment.
Historically enormous (a Kasparov revival weapon in the 1990s); teaches genuinely different development-for-tempo strategy than the quiet Giuoco lines. Clearly standalone by every test.

entries.fullName: Two Knights Defense: Fried Liver Attack
entries.notes: One of the most famous named attacking sacrifices in club-level chess; requires precise follow-up to justify the piece and teaches king-hunt technique distinct from the rest of the Italian complex. Clearly standalone despite deep nesting.

entries.fullName: Italian Game: Giuoco Piano, Giuoco Pianissimo
entries.notes: The dominant modern practical choice in the Italian complex at every level from club to elite (used as a low-theory, high-technique weapon much like the Berlin). Distinct enough in plans and pace from the sharper c3/d4 Giuoco Piano to merit its own entry despite nesting under it.

This IS the main line the italian-game lesson teaches (3...Bc5 mirroring White's bishop); kept as a named branch entry for search rather than a duplicate standalone lesson. Giuoco Pianissimo (4.d3) is promoted to its own standalone entry given its modern importance.

Solid but passive; Black avoids theory at the cost of activity. Real name, occasional club practice, but not different enough from the general Italian Game picture to justify a standalone lesson — covered as a sideline within italian-game.

structures: e4/e5 or d4 isolani after exchanges
entries.notes: The most natural developing try after 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6; umbrella family for Giuoco Piano, Evans Gambit, and Two Knights Defense. Four Knights Italian (4.Bc4 in the Four Knights move order) transposes here.

Sacrifices two pieces for three pawns and an exposed king; objectively unsound against accurate defense despite a cult online following and real search traffic under its name. Kept only for search-honesty, per the joke/dubious-opening rule.

motifs: ...Ng4 mating nets against a king on f-file
entries.notes: Black ignores the attacked f7 pawn and counterattacks f2 instead — genuinely unique strategic idea (offering rather than avoiding complications) and a famous name (Wilkes-Barre in US/UK usage) that amateurs search for by name.

structures: early piece skirmishes before pawn structure settles
entries.notes: Black meets 3.Bc4 with development instead of symmetry, inviting the sharp 4.Ng5 lines (Fried Liver Attack, Traxler Counterattack) that define the opening's character. Distinct enough in temperament from Giuoco Piano to be its own standalone entry; no lesson written yet.

Almost pure move-order flexibility: 1.g3 very often transposes into the Réti, King's Indian Attack, or (with an early c4/d4) the Catalan; kept as its own entry because the g3-first move order is a distinct, commonly named practical choice (Gedeon Barcza used it as a whole system), but most of its content is genuinely transpositional rather than independent theory. 'Hungarian Opening' and 'King's Fianchetto Opening' are used interchangeably for 1.g3 in English-language sources.

motifs: ...e4 pawn thrust gaining space and tempo
open e-file pin/pressure against White's king
structures: open center with Black often ahead in development for the gambitted pawn
entries.notes: A historically major and philosophically distinct reply — instead of grabbing White's f-pawn, Black counter-strikes the center immediately. Teaches counterattacking principle as clearly as the Albin or Scandinavian countergambits do elsewhere in the catalog.

entries.fullName: King's Gambit Accepted: Modern Defense (Fischer Defense)
entries.notes: Bobby Fischer's famous 1961 'A Bust to the King's Gambit' recommendation (...d6 preparing ...g5 to hold the extra pawn); culturally significant name worth surfacing in search, but the underlying idea is simple enough to teach as a sideline within the main kings-gambit lesson rather than its own study.

structures: locked kingside pawns (h4/g4) versus open center
entries.notes: The main 'sound' branch of the classical KGA main line (h4/Ne5), tied to the Immortal Game lineage; real historical and instructive weight distinct from the all-in Muzio.

The quintessential 19th-century attacking gambit (Immortal Game, Evergreen Game lineage); heavy modern theory has reduced elite practice but it remains a rich teaching vehicle for attacking principles and a real surprise weapon at every other level.

The main-line acceptance the kings-gambit lesson is built around; kept as a named branch rather than a duplicate standalone entry. Its most famous named sub-gambits (Kieseritzky, Muzio) are promoted to their own entries below given how distinct and independently studied each is.

entries.fullName: King's Gambit: King's Gambit Declined, Classical Variation
entries.notes: Genuinely different strategic approach from the Accepted lines: Black keeps the extra central pawn structure intact and targets White's weakened kingside rather than entering sacrificial theory.

themes: full piece sacrifice for permanent attack
structures: Black up a full piece, White with total development lead and open lines
entries.notes: Sacrifices a whole knight (not recaptured) purely for attacking chances — the archetypal romantic-chess gambit and a name every serious student of chess history encounters, even though it sees almost no modern top-level practice.

motifs: exposed Black king after early f-pawn advance
entries.notes: Objectively considered dubious with best play (Black weakens the king for counterplay White can often decline into a safe advantage), but it has a genuine dedicated following, its own theory, and real historical pedigree (also called the Greco Countergambit) — real enough for historical tier, not a joke line.

structures: universal fianchetto setup vs any White center
entries.notes: Catalogued as a separate family from the Pirc Defense per editorial convention: Black delays or omits ...Nf6 to keep maximum flexibility, choosing structures only after seeing White's setup. The two families are close cousins joined by frequent transposition.

Named for Bukhuti Gurgenidze; aims for a quick central ...d5 strike. Reached at least as often via the Caro-Kann move order (1.e4 c6 2.d4 d5 3.Nc3 g6), so catalogued here as a branch of the Modern Defense with a cross-reference to its Caro-Kann sibling rather than as an independent standalone.

Brings the queen out early with no real threat (apocryphally attributed to Napoleon Bonaparte, who was a weak player); objectively poor by modern standards but a real, plausibly-searched historical curiosity name — kept only for search-honesty.

motifs: Bb2 pressure down the long diagonal
entries.notes: Named for Aron Nimzowitsch's early advocacy and Bent Larsen's championing of it at the top level (including vs Spassky, 'Match of the Century' 1970); real, continuing elite practice (Carlsen has used it repeatedly), which secures major tier despite its flank-opening reputation. MUST-include entry per scope.

structures: knight-first setup, central structure decided late
entries.notes: A legitimate if rare try, named for Aron Nimzowitsch, developing the knight before committing a central pawn to keep structural options open. Occasional strong modern practice as a surprise weapon justifies specialized rather than historical status.

motifs: Bb7 pressure on the long diagonal
entries.notes: Named for 19th-century English amateur John Owen. Genuine historical pedigree and an occasional surprise weapon, but negligible top-level frequency today — retained as an honest historical entry rather than a mainstream defense.

themes: knight sacrifice to wreck Black's king safety
engine-era reassessment of an old idea
structures: White trades a knight for two pawns and lasting initiative
entries.notes: A 19th-century idea (John Cochrane) that has seen genuine 21st-century revival as a practical surprise weapon, including at grandmaster level, specifically because engines rate the resulting long-term compensation more highly than earlier generations believed.

themes: drawish reputation as a practical weapon
motifs: d4 central break for White (3.d4, Steinitz/Classical lines)
structures: simplified endgame-leaning structures in main lines
entries.notes: Black mirrors White's knight development and meets central threats with equal and opposite counterplay; a top-level equalizing weapon (comparable in spirit to the Berlin) and a name every serious amateur will encounter.

motifs: White's d4 break against a cramped Black setup
structures: Philidor pawn chain (d6/e5 versus White's e4/d4)
entries.notes: One of the oldest named defenses in chess (analyzed by François-André Danican Philidor in the 18th century); solid and low-theory but concedes space, making it a useful teaching case for the tradeoff between solidity and activity.

motifs: Bh6 trade of the dark-squared bishop
structures: White queenside castling vs Black kingside fianchetto
entries.notes: Named for its popularity around English club (150 BCF-grade) level; a simple, ambitious system (Be3/Qd2/f3, O-O-O and h4-h5) that sidesteps heavy Austrian Attack theory. Real, common practical weapon, hence standalone rather than folded into the family entry.

entries.moves: 1.e4 d6 2.d4 Nf6 3.Nc3 g6 4.f4 Bg7 5.Nf3 O-O 6.Bd3 c5
structures: White f4/e4/d4 big center vs g6 fianchetto
entries.notes: White's most ambitious and theoretically critical try against the Pirc, grabbing full center with f4 aiming at e5. Distinct strategic character and deep independent theory earn it standalone status despite living under the Pirc umbrella.

entries.fullName: Pirc Defense: Classical Variation (Two Knights System)
structures: restrained center, classical development vs fianchetto
entries.notes: White's solid main developing scheme (Nf3/Be2/O-O) as a positional alternative to the sharper Austrian Attack; common enough at club and master level to merit its own entry.

Delays or omits ...g6 for an early ...c6 (Josef Pribyl), blending Pirc and Caro-Kann move orders with plans like ...Qa5 and ...b5. A recognized name worth surfacing in search, but does not carry enough independent strategic weight to warrant a standalone lesson beyond the Pirc family entry.

structures: big White center vs g6 fianchetto
entries.notes: Umbrella family for the ...d6/...Nf6/...g6 setup vs 1.e4. Catalogued separately from the Modern Defense (which delays ...Nf6 for maximum flexibility) and shares deep transpositional kinship with the King's Indian Defense.

themes: early piece activity over material symmetry
entries.notes: Nicknamed 'Orangutan' after Tartakower reportedly consulted an orangutan at the Bronx Zoo before playing it (New York 1924); 'Sokolsky' honors Alexei Sokolsky's monograph on the line. Real if uncommon serious practice; objectively a bit loose against precise play (1...e5 hits the b4-pawn immediately) but a legitimate system with its own plans, not a joke opening.

motifs: d4 central break supported by c3
structures: White's c3 pawn limits the Nb1 development square
entries.notes: A real, named, low-theory alternative to 3.Bc4/3.d4/3.Bb5 with its own logic (supporting d4 while keeping options open); legitimate club-level weapon, never fashionable at the top.

themes: Ruy Lopez ideas without committing the knight to f3
move-order flexibility keeping f4 in reserve
motifs: transposition traps into favorable Ruy/Italian structures
structures: structures often resolving toward Ruy Lopez-like formations
entries.notes: Described by Graham Burgess as looking like 'a Ruy Lopez where White has forgotten to play 2.Nf3'; not as bad as it first looks (keeps f4 options alive) but genuinely rare, with only minor practice — real historical/niche value, not a joke line.
Standalone major: historically important countergambit with a genuinely different strategic idea (an advanced, cramping black d-pawn) and real trap-based teaching value (the classic Lasker Trap).

Real, occasionally seen at strong-amateur/GM surprise-weapon level (develops the light bishop outside the pawn chain before committing to ...c6/...e6), but low frequency and thin enough to fold into the general Queen's Gambit fundamentals lesson as a named 'other second move' rather than its own study.

themes: combines Queen's Gambit central play with Indian-style piece pressure
motifs: Bg2 pressure down the long diagonal
Qa4/Qc2 recovering the c4 pawn in Open lines
structures: IQP in some Open Catalan lines
entries.notes: Standalone core: parented under the Queen's Gambit family here since Black's central ...d5 typically produces genuine Queen's Gambit-family structures with an added fianchetto; ECO classifies it under the Indian 'E' codes (E00-E09) and it is equally reachable via 1.Nf3/1.c4 Reti/English move orders and the Queen's Indian/Nimzo-Indian complex — those alternate routes are recorded via related/transposesTo per ontology rule 2.

themes: maintaining the center rather than grabbing a pawn
small persistent edge for White from the fianchetto bishop
structures: eventual hanging pawns or IQP if tension resolves
entries.notes: Standalone major: the solid, positional counterpart to the Open Catalan — Black keeps the extra central pawn tension rather than grabbing c4, leading to long strategic maneuvering battles that are a distinct lesson from the Open lines' concrete pawn-grab theory.

themes: temporary pawn sacrifice against the fianchetto bishop
White's long-term compensation on the long diagonal
motifs: Qa4+ picking up the c4 pawn
b3/Bb2 or Rd1 pressure to justify the pawn investment
structures: Catalan bishop vs. Black's queenside pawn majority
entries.notes: Standalone major: Black accepts the pawn for counterplay, producing a genuinely distinct strategic battle (piece pressure vs. extra pawn) compared to the Closed Catalan's maneuvering game.

motifs: Bg4/Bf5 pinning or contesting White's center
structures: asymmetrical, often doubled/broken pawns for Black
entries.notes: Standalone specialized: unorthodox but genuinely distinct defense (develops the queen's knight before committing the center), historically championed by Chigorin and revived in modern practice by players such as Morozevich; legitimate surprise weapon with real theory.

Named after Frank Marshall but considered structurally dubious (allows 3.cxd5 Nxd5 4.e4 gaining a full tempo/center for White); kept in the catalog for search-honesty and folded into the general Queen's Gambit lesson as a minor, not-recommended try, without its own study.

Root family node for the entire Queen's Gambit complex (QGD, QGA, Slav, Semi-Slav, Tarrasch, Chigorin, Albin, and Catalan as a closely related g3 system). Not a true gambit — White regains the c-pawn in virtually all main lines; kept as openingType 'gambit' for historical/naming continuity.

Standalone core defense: Black hands back central control temporarily for quick development and queenside pawn play; distinct strategic content from QGD (White almost always regains the pawn, so the fight is over tempo and structure, not material).

White grabs the full center immediately instead of the quieter 3.Nf3. Real but secondary try; covered inside the main QGA lesson rather than as its own study. branchOfLessonId is a forward reference to the QGA entry's future lessonId (not yet assigned) — orchestrator should confirm once queens-gambit-accepted's study exists.

themes: piece development behind a firm pawn chain
entries.notes: The classical umbrella defense; covers Orthodox/Lasker/Tartakower/Cambridge Springs/Exchange/Ragozin/Semi-Tarrasch/Vienna as its named children. Existing study covers the family fundamentals; several children below merit their own standalone studies.

entries.fullName: Queen's Gambit Declined: Cambridge Springs Defense
entries.moves: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Nbd7 5.e3 c6 6.Nf3 Qa5
themes: tactical resource against careless White play
entries.notes: Standalone: distinct move order (...Nbd7 and ...c6 before ...Be7) built around the sharp ...Qa5 idea, with real practical sting and a famous historical origin; parented directly under QGD since it deviates from the Orthodox ...Be7 tree at move 4.

themes: symmetrical pawn structure with imbalanced plans
entries.notes: Standalone (leans standalone per the test): the textbook home of the Carlsbad structure and minority attack — arguably the single most instructive QGD structure for teaching pawn-structure planning, independent of whether the resulting middlegame 'feels' sharp.

entries.fullName: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Lasker Variation
entries.moves: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7 5.e3 O-O 6.Nf3 h6 7.Bh4 Ne4
entries.notes: Real, well-known drawing-oriented plan (early ...Ne4 forcing simplifying trades) with a distinct idea but narrow scope compared to Tartakower/Cambridge Springs; judged branch-only, taught inside the Orthodox Defense lesson. branchOfLessonId is a forward reference pending that entry's own lessonId.

themes: central tension resolved by White's choice
entries.notes: Standalone: the historic main-line tree of QGD (Capablanca, Alekhine, Botvinnik-era battleground) with genuinely distinct strategic content from the Exchange/Ragozin/Tarrasch branches. Parent umbrella for Lasker, Tartakower, and Cambridge Springs, each of which earns its own entry below.

Standalone (leans standalone per the test): a serious, modern, heavily-analyzed defense in its own right, distinct enough from mainline QGD to deserve separate treatment. Ancestry note: reachable via either QGD move order (2...e6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Nf3 Bb4, as parented here) or the Nimzo-Indian move order (1.d4 Nf6 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Bb4 4.Nf3 d5) — per ontology rule 2 we keep QGD as the single parent and record the Nimzo-Indian route via transposesTo/related.

themes: piece activity compensating for structural weakness
entries.notes: Standalone: distinct from the full Tarrasch Defense (Black delays ...c5 until after ...Nf6, avoiding an isolated d-pawn of his own by capturing on d5 with the knight instead of a pawn); serious, well-tested defense used at the highest level (Kasparov, Kramnik).

entries.fullName: Queen's Gambit Declined: Orthodox Defense, Tartakower Variation
entries.moves: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Bg5 Be7 5.e3 O-O 6.Nf3 h6 7.Bh4 b6
themes: isolated d-pawn vs. hanging pawns transformations
entries.notes: Standalone major: enormously popular at elite level (Kramnik and others) with a genuinely distinct strategic plan (early queenside fianchetto instead of central resolution) — clears the standalone test easily.

Sharp, well-defined sideline (immediate ...dxc4 and ...Bb4 against 4.Bg5) with real but limited modern practice; judged branch-only rather than standalone, folded into the main QGD lesson. ECO code is an approximate best guess (D39, shared neighborhood with the Ragozin's ...Bb4 ideas) — flagged for orchestrator verification.

themes: some of the sharpest theory in classical chess
fight over the c4/e4 pawn breaks
motifs: dxc4 followed by ...b5 to hold the pawn
piece-sacrifice lines in the Botvinnik System
entries.notes: Standalone core: combines ...c6 and ...e6, reachable from either the Slav move order (2...c6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Nf3 e6, as parented here) or the QGD move order (2...e6 3.Nc3 c6); per ontology rule 2 we keep Slav as the single parent and note the QGD route via related/transposesTo. One of the most theoretically dense defenses in the entire d4 complex, home to the Meran, Botvinnik, and Moscow systems.

entries.moves: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Nf3 e6 5.Bg5 dxc4 6.e4 b5 7.e5 h6 8.Bh4 g5 9.Nxg5 hxg5 10.Bxg5
themes: piece sacrifice for a mass of connected passed pawns
some of the sharpest, most forcing theory in all of chess
motifs: Black's connected queenside passers vs. White's piece activity
entries.notes: Standalone specialized (Anti-Meran/Botvinnik grouped as one entry per the editorial judgment call): the 5.Bg5 dxc4 piece-sacrifice tabiya, introduced in the 1945 USSR-USA radio match; one of the most famous and forcing theoretical duels in chess, clearly deserving its own study despite (or because of) its narrow, heavily-forced move order.

entries.moves: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Nf3 e6 5.e3 Nbd7 6.Bd3 dxc4 7.Bxc4 b5
themes: dynamic piece play against White's center
one of the most famous main lines in classical chess
entries.notes: Standalone core: legendary main line (5.e3 approach) with immense practical and historical significance, entirely distinct in character from the sharp piece-sacrifice Anti-Meran/Botvinnik lines.

entries.moves: 1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6 3.Nc3 Nf6 4.Nf3 e6 5.Bg5 h6 6.Bxf6 Qxf6
themes: solid, calmer alternative to the Botvinnik chaos
queen recapture on f6 keeping the position simple
structures: flexible, less committal center than the Meran
entries.notes: Standalone specialized: a real, distinct elite-level choice (5...h6 6.Bxf6) offering a solid alternative to both the razor-sharp Botvinnik and the heavily-theorized Meran; deliberately opposite in character to the Botvinnik Variation, which is the point of teaching them separately.

structures: flexible, not yet committed — can transpose to several Slav/Semi-Slav pawn structures
entries.notes: Standalone specialized: a genuinely modern strategic idea (popularized by Chebanenko and Bologan) — deliberately postponing the main structural decision to deny White clear targets; distinct enough in plan from the Main Line to teach separately.

themes: solid structure without shutting in the light bishop
motifs: ...Bf5 developing outside the pawn chain before ...e6
entries.notes: Standalone core: the key structural alternative to QGD ...e6 — solves the classic 'bad light-squared bishop' problem of the QGD by developing Bf5/Bg4 before playing ...e6. One of the most reliable and heavily played defenses to 1.d4 at every level.

themes: no minority attack for White (queenside pawns already traded)
maneuvering battles, often drawish reputation but real technique required
structures: Carlsbad-adjacent but without the c-pawn minority
entries.notes: Standalone: distinct from the QGD Exchange Variation because the symmetrical c/d-pawn structure removes White's minority attack entirely, shifting the fight to piece play and small structural nuances (a genuinely different lesson than Carlsbad minority-attack technique).

themes: accepted-pawn structure with active bishop already developed
a4/Ne5 fights over the Bf5 bishop
structures: extra queenside space for Black after holding c4/b5 ideas
entries.notes: Standalone: the traditional main tabiya of the Slav (also historically called the Czech Variation since it developed largely through Czech players' contributions); one combined entry rather than two, since both names describe essentially the same 4...dxc4 5.a4 Bf5 tree — flagged for orchestrator review in case a finer split is wanted.

Real named sideline (fianchetto setup instead of ...Bf5), occasionally seen, but narrow enough to fold into the main Slav lesson rather than stand alone. ECO range is a broad approximation pending a more specific sub-code lookup.

themes: isolated queen pawn as a dynamic asset
motifs: Bg5 pin on Nf6 to pressure the IQP
entries.notes: Standalone core: a famous, historically pivotal defense (Tarrasch's 'hanging pawns are strong' doctrine vs. the classical school) with genuinely different strategic content — Black voluntarily accepts an IQP for piece activity and open lines, the opposite plan from mainline QGD.

Honest tier: a real, historically significant gambit (Armand Blackmar 1882, developed by Emil Diemer) with deep amateur theory and a devoted following, but modern engine analysis holds that accurate defense (e.g. the Euwe Defense, 4...e6/...c6 setups) gives Black a durable extra pawn without full compensation. Kept at 'specialized' rather than 'historical' because it remains a genuinely practiced, actively theorized weapon today, not a museum piece — but claims of full/objective compensation are not supported and are avoided in lesson framing.

entries.moves: 1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e3 e6 4.Bd3 c5 5.c3 Nc6 6.Nbd2 Bd6 7.O-O O-O 8.e4
entries.notes: The 'classic' Colle: c3 support point, delayed e3-e4 break behind full development. Named branch of the colle-system lesson, not a standalone — the strategic content overlaps too heavily with the parent to justify its own study.
Moves stop at the common branch point (4.Bd3); the two named continuations (c3 vs b3) are modeled as branches per the requested scope.

entries.moves: 1.d4 d5 2.Nf3 Nf6 3.e3 e6 4.Bd3 c5 5.b3 Nc6 6.Bb2 Bd6 7.O-O O-O 8.Nbd2
entries.notes: Adds a second fianchettoed bishop on b2 for extra pressure on the long diagonal and typically a sharper Ne5-based kingside plan than the plain Koltanowski line. Named and recognizable enough to list, but shares the Colle skeleton — branch, not standalone.

Honest tier: objectively unsound against accurate defense (e.g. 4.Bf4 or 4.Nc3 holding the extra pawn comfortably), and its entire practical value is springing memorized traps on unprepared opponents. Kept at 'historical' (not excluded) because it has a real name, real if thin tournament history, and is commonly searched for by beginners who lost a scholastic game to it.

Judgment call: kept standalone rather than folded into london-system. Early Nc3 (before Nf3) changes the strategic character meaningfully — it commits to a more aggressive e4 push and accepts a knight can be met with ...Nxc3, unlike the quiet Colle-like main London. Real modern top-level practice (Jobava, Grischuk and others) and a distinct enough plan set clear the standalone bar at 'specialized' rather than 'core'.
Existing standalone lesson (catalogCode O006). The single most popular 1.d4 system at club level; core tier is not in doubt.

themes: avoiding heavy Queen's Gambit / Indian theory
entries.notes: Umbrella navigation node for White's 1.d4 tries that deliberately sidestep the Queen's Gambit / Catalan / Indian main-line complex (covered in other fragments). Groups the setup-based 'systems' — London, Colle, Torre, Trompowsky, Veresov, Stonewall Attack, Blackmar-Diemer — under one navigable ECO A40-A46/D00 umbrella. Not itself a distinct lesson; the value is purely organizational.
Legitimate if less common than Trompowsky/Torre; committing Nc3 early blocks White's own c-pawn, which is the main practical drawback and the reason it sits at 'specialized' rather than 'major'.

This is White's own Stonewall setup (d4/e3/f4/c3), distinct from the Black Dutch Stonewall (dutch-defense-stonewall) which mirrors the same skeleton one file over with reversed colors — the two should never be merged despite the shared name and near-identical pawn shape. Editorially 'specialized' rather than 'major': real club-level following and genuine structural teaching value, but a smaller and more dated repertoire than London/Colle/Torre/Trompowsky.
Named for Carlos Torre (also historically called Ruth Opening after Adolf Ruth, who played it first but did not develop its theory).

structures: doubled f-pawns for Black after Bxf6
entries.notes: A serious, well-theorized surprise weapon at every level (Julian Hodgson's signature opening); avoids nearly all King's Indian / Nimzo-Indian / Grünfeld theory in one move.

Family root and existing beginner lesson. It is built around the 3...a6 (Morphy Defense) main line through the classical c3/d4 break, and covers Berlin, Exchange, and Open lines as branch commentary within that single lesson — even though each of those also earns its own catalog entry below for search and taxonomy purposes.

entries.fullName: Ruy Lopez: Closed Defense, Anti-Marshall Systems
entries.moves: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 a6 4.Ba4 Nf6 5.O-O Be7 6.Re1 b5 7.Bb3 O-O 8.a4
entries.notes: Not one line but a family of White 8th-move tries (8.a4, 8.h3, 8.d3, and other move-order shifts) whose entire point is sidestepping 8.c3 d5 and the Marshall Attack. Best taught as 'the other side of the coin' inside a Marshall Attack lesson rather than as its own standalone study; the move shown (8.a4) is only the most common representative.

entries.fullName: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Archangelsk Variation
entries.moves: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 a6 4.Ba4 Nf6 5.O-O b5 6.Bb3 Bb7
structures: Archangel bishop pair aimed at White's king
entries.notes: Groups the classical Archangelsk (...Bb7) and Modern/Neo-Archangelsk (...Bc5 instead of ...Be7) tries under one entry: both skip the quiet ...Be7/...d6 setup for immediate queenside space and active piece play, championed at various points by Shirov, Svidler, and Nepomniachtchi. Distinct enough in move order and character from both the Closed and Marshall complexes to stand alone.

Kramnik's weapon against Kasparov in their 2000 world championship match turned this into one of the most important defenses in modern elite chess. The queenless 'Berlin Wall' endgame (4.O-O Nxe4 5.d4 Nd6 6.Bxc6 dxc6 7.dxe5 Nf5 8.Qxd8+ Kxd8) is famously hard to convert despite White's structural edge — different enough in structure and plans from the Morphy/Closed complex, and important enough, to warrant its own future lesson even though the existing family lesson introduces it briefly.
H.E. Bird's eccentric immediate challenge to the Spanish bishop. Rare above club level and carries known tactical pitfalls for Black, but not enough independent theory for a standalone lesson.

entries.fullName: Ruy Lopez: Closed Defense, Breyer Variation
entries.moves: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 a6 4.Ba4 Nf6 5.O-O Be7 6.Re1 b5 7.Bb3 O-O 8.c3 d6 9.h3 Nb8
entries.notes: Gyula Breyer's paradoxical retreat (the knight returns to b8 to reroute via d7) was once mocked, then became one of Karpov's signature systems and a modern engine favorite. Real depth, but still treated as a named sub-branch of the Closed complex for this catalog.

entries.fullName: Ruy Lopez: Closed Defense, Chigorin Variation
entries.moves: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 a6 4.Ba4 Nf6 5.O-O Be7 6.Re1 b5 7.Bb3 O-O 8.c3 d6 9.h3 Na5 10.Bc2 c5 11.d4 Qc7
entries.notes: Named for Mikhail Chigorin; one of the classical main systems of the Closed Ruy Lopez (the ...Na5/...c5/...Qc7 complex, including its Yugoslav sub-branch). At this depth it belongs inside a future Closed Ruy Lopez lesson rather than as its own standalone study.

Develops actively but allows White favorable central breaks (c3 and d4 hit the bishop with tempo). Seen occasionally at club level and worth naming for search, but without enough independent modern theory for a standalone lesson.

entries.fullName: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Closed Defense
entries.moves: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 a6 4.Ba4 Nf6 5.O-O Be7 6.Re1 b5 7.Bb3 O-O 8.c3 d6
entries.notes: The classical main-line battleground the existing beginner lesson introduces (through 9...c5 10.d4). This entry represents the vast deeper body of grandmaster theory beyond that lesson's scope — the named 9th-move systems (Chigorin, Breyer, Zaitsev) branch from here, as does the Marshall Attack at move 8. Warrants its own future intermediate/advanced lesson distinct from the introductory family study.
Very rare, mostly of antiquarian interest (named for 18th-century Italian analyst Carlo Cozio). Kept in the catalog for search-honesty only.

Fischer's famous revival (5.O-O then d4, playing against Black's crippled queenside majority) turned this into a serious, structurally distinct weapon rather than a mere simplification. The existing family lesson already walks through why 4.Bxc6 followed by Nxe5 does not simply win a pawn; the Exchange plan's long-term endgame strategy deserves its own separate lesson.

Associated with Vasily Smyslov; a genuinely distinct fianchetto idea but rare enough in serious practice that it stays a named branch rather than its own lesson. See ruy-lopez-fianchetto-deferred for the more commonly played ...a6-first version.

entries.fullName: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Fianchetto Defense Deferred (Smyslov Deferred)
entries.notes: The more commonly seen version of Smyslov's fianchetto idea, played after securing ...a6 first. Still a minor branch relative to mainstream Closed and Open theory, so it points back to the family lesson rather than the not-yet-standalone Morphy Defense node.

entries.fullName: Ruy Lopez: Closed Defense, Marshall Attack
entries.moves: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 a6 4.Ba4 Nf6 5.O-O Be7 6.Re1 b5 7.Bb3 O-O 8.c3 d5
themes: long-term piece activity for a pawn
structures: open e-file with White's king exposed
entries.notes: Frank Marshall's prepared piece sacrifice (unveiled against Capablanca in 1918, though Capablanca reportedly had advance warning and still defended accurately) is one of the most famous forcing gambits in chess, with decades of engine-checked theory on both sides. Serious, culturally famous, and strategically distinct enough from ordinary Closed Ruy Lopez play to be its own entry even though it grows directly out of the Closed tabiya at move 8.

Black's most popular reply for over 150 years, named for Paul Morphy. It is the exact spine of the existing ruy-lopez lesson (built around 3...a6 through move 10), so this node exists for taxonomy/search completeness rather than as a distinct future lesson.

entries.fullName: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Norwegian Variation
entries.notes: Immediately hunts the b3-bishop rather than waiting for the c3/Re1/h3 preparation of mainline Closed Ruy Lopez play. Known since the 1880s and revived by Taimanov (and played occasionally by Anand, Topalov, and Sokolov), but time-costly and long superseded by the delayed ...Na5 of main theory. A nice pedagogical echo of the family lesson's own ...Na5 idea, played four moves too early — worth naming, not worth its own lesson.

entries.fullName: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Open Variation
motifs: d4-d5 push while the knight sits on e4
entries.notes: Black grabs e4 and accepts a temporary lead in White's development in exchange for lasting piece activity — a completely different strategic character from the Closed main line, with its own deep sub-theory (Riga Variation, Dilworth Variation). The existing family lesson only shows the basic tactical point (5...Nxe4 6.d4); it does not cover this independent body of theory, which is why Open Ruy Lopez earns its own future lesson.

An immediate, provocative bid for counterplay against e4 before Black finishes developing. Sound enough for club and occasional grandmaster practice, but it demands precise tactical preparation, so it stays a specialized rather than mainstream reply.

World Champion Wilhelm Steinitz's solid but passive try. Largely superseded once players realized inserting 3...a6 first (the Modern/Deferred Steinitz) reaches the same structure with a useful extra tempo on the bishop. Kept for historical and educational value, not competitive currency.

entries.fullName: Ruy Lopez: Morphy Defense, Modern Steinitz Defense
structures: e5 chain with the ...a6 tempo already banked
entries.notes: The practical, tempo-improved version of the old Steinitz idea; a genuine solid repertoire choice used occasionally by Kramnik and Anand, and distinct from the immediate 3...d6 which loses a tempo to a later ...a6.

entries.fullName: Ruy Lopez: Closed Defense, Zaitsev Variation
entries.moves: 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bb5 a6 4.Ba4 Nf6 5.O-O Be7 6.Re1 b5 7.Bb3 O-O 8.c3 d6 9.h3 Bb7
entries.notes: Kasparov's long-time main weapon (...Bb7 keeps the c8-bishop flexible before committing it). Another deep named system nested inside the Closed complex rather than a standalone entry.

motifs: Nc3/Nf3 tempo gains on the black queen
queenside vs. kingside recapture choice (...Qxd5 vs. ...Nf6)
structures: open center, no fixed pawn chain
entries.notes: New family entry; no existing lesson. Long dismissed as passive, now a respected top-level choice (Carlsen, Caruana, Nepomniachtchi); the family's honest teaching point is the tempo economics of recapturing on d5 with a piece a move early.

entries.fullName: Scandinavian Defense: Modern Variation, Icelandic Gambit
themes: second pawn sacrifice for development and open lines
motifs: rapid piece mobilization for two pawns
entries.notes: Claims discipline: compensation for the second pawn is considered objectively insufficient with accurate defense, but the line is a real, frequently-searched named gambit with genuine practical sting at club level — kept as a branch with an honest status note rather than excluded.

motifs: rapid piece development for the pawn
structures: open center, no fixed pawn chain
entries.notes: Genuinely different strategy from the Qxd5 lines: Black delays recapturing material in favor of piece activity, occasionally not recapturing the pawn at all in gambit sub-lines. Distinct enough in plan and risk profile to merit its own standalone entry.

entries.fullName: Scandinavian Defense: Modern Variation, Portuguese Variation
entries.notes: Real, sound-ish practical gambit with dedicated theory; kept as a branch of the Modern Variation rather than standalone given its narrower scope.

themes: queen safety on the a5-e1 diagonal
structures: open center, no fixed pawn chain
entries.notes: Judgment call: the assignment allows Qa5/Qd6 as branches or standalone; both are given standalone status here as the two primary, genuinely distinct modern main-line choices (differing queen files, different plans against Nb5/Nd5 jumps). Flagging for orchestrator review. The 3.Nc3 trunk is folded directly into this entry rather than given its own node, since 3.Nc3 is White's near-universal reply to 2...Qxd5.

structures: open center, no fixed pawn chain
entries.notes: The currently preferred top-level main line (Carlsen among its champions): the queen avoids the tempo-loss tricks that plague 3...Qa5 (no Bd2/Nb5 hit) at the cost of blocking the d-pawn temporarily. Named the 'Bronstein Variation' by some sources — a different Bronstein reference than the Caro-Kann's Bronstein-Larsen; kept as alias only, not conflated.

motifs: c3-recapture gambit idea shared with Danish Gambit
structures: White often two pawns down for a large lead in development
entries.notes: A real 19th-century gambit (named for Carl Theodor Göring) still seen at club level; never fashionable at the top but distinct enough from the Scotch Gambit's single-pawn approach (c3 recapture idea, kin to the Danish Gambit) to stand on its own.

themes: Italian-style piece play with an extra tempo
structures: White ahead in development, down a pawn
entries.notes: Popular club-level and engine-friendly gambit that trades the extra pawn for fast, simple development — a good beginner-to-intermediate attacking template.

Kasparov's 1990s revival made it a top-level main weapon again after decades of being considered a mild sideline; strikes the center a move earlier than the Italian/Ruy, producing genuinely different structures.
Delays ...d6 so White cannot play the sharp Yugoslav Attack; White's critical try is the Maroczy Bind (c4+Nc3+Be2), a structure this entry, not a separate opening, per editorial convention.

White's most popular practical way to sidestep Open Sicilian theory entirely while still fighting for the center with c3+d4; leads to well-known IQP structures similar in spirit to some Caro-Kann/French positions.

Navigation-only umbrella: unlike Open Sicilian, Anti-Sicilians has no single characteristic move order or structure to teach as one lesson — Alapin, Closed, Grand Prix, Rossolimo, Moscow, Smith-Morra, and Wing Gambit are each independently standalone with genuinely different plans. This node exists purely to group them for browsing; its moves field intentionally matches the family root since it spans many second-move tries. Mentioned briefly inside the Sicilian Defense root lesson as 'ways White avoids the Open Sicilian.'

The most 'natural-development' Sicilian setup; largely subsumed today by the Richter-Rauzer (5...Nc6 6.Bg5) and Boleslavsky/Sveshnikov-adjacent structures, but the named Classical Variation remains a recognized standalone system with real modern practice.
Avoids d4 entirely, playing a King's-Indian-style setup with colors reversed; structurally the mirror image of the King's English (1.c4 e5) with an extra tempo.

Family root; existing lesson already teaches the shared Open Sicilian structure (c-for-d trade, half-open c-file) underneath all named variations. English Opening is the reversed-color cousin of the same asymmetry idea.
Named for the pawn skeleton's resemblance to a dragon's outline. The Yugoslav Attack (opposite-side castling races) makes it one of the sharpest, most theory-dense lines in all of chess.

All four knights developed by move five; solid and fairly drawish at high levels, real but modest modern practice. Standalone by name recognition but limited independent theory beyond transposing into Taimanov-type middlegames.

Named for its popularity on the 1980s English 'Grand Prix' club circuit; a direct kingside-attacking try that can arise via 2.Nc3 and 3.f4 or the more direct 2.f4 move order (both covered under this entry).

Delays even ...Nc6, aiming to meet 3.c4 (Maroczy) with ...Bg7 and ...Nc6/...Nf6 flexibly, sidestepping some Maroczy move orders. A recognized name but not distinct enough in plans from the Accelerated Dragon to warrant its own lesson.

Same ...e5 hole-on-d5 bargain as the Sveshnikov but reached without ...Nf6 first, giving White the extra Nb5-d6+ resource. The 19th-century name Löwenthal Variation is treated as a historical alias here rather than a separate entry — modern theory and the Kalashnikov largely cover the same ground with refined move orders.
...a6 prevents Nb5 and keeps the knight-development square choice (c6 vs. d7) open longest of any e6 Sicilian; often transposes into Taimanov structures.

A King's-Indian-Attack-style d3/g3/Bg2/O-O setup against any Black reply, popularized by IM Danny Kopec as a low-theory club-level system. Same strategic family as the Closed Sicilian; not distinct enough to justify a standalone lesson.

structures: Open Sicilian center (if White later plays d4)
entries.notes: The Rossolimo's counterpart against 2...d6 move orders; often transposes into similar structures. Popularized in Soviet-era Moscow practice, hence the name.
The most played opening in top-level chess for decades (Fischer, Kasparov). ...a6 is a waiting/prophylactic move enabling ...e5 or ...e6 setups and queenside expansion with tempo.

Attacks e4 before committing to ...d6 or ...Nc6; named for Aron Nimzowitsch, its most famous early practitioner. Real but occasional practice at all levels, deserving its own entry per the standalone test (distinct move-two idea, recognizable name).
Named for Belgian GM Alberic O'Kelly de Galway; a genuine try-order weapon (dodges Rossolimo/Moscow 3.Bb5(+) ideas) that usually transposes to Open Sicilian or Kan structures after 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4.

Standalone umbrella lesson: after 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 every named variation (Najdorf, Dragon, Scheveningen, Taimanov, etc.) shares this structure and the tempo-for-development bargain. Justifies its own structures/plans lesson above the individual variation lessons rather than being purely navigational, per the family's existing content plan.

...Bb4 pins the c3-knight instead of the more common ...Nc6 or ...a6, immediately contesting e4; a recognized named idea within the e6-Sicilian complex, taught inside the Taimanov lesson rather than standalone.
Named for Nicolas Rossolimo; a top-level favorite for decades as a low-theory, high-practical-value way to avoid deep Open Sicilian preparation while retaining real winning chances.

Named for a 1923 Scheveningen tournament; the flexible d6+e6 pawn duo is the model 'small center' Sicilian structure and underlies Kasparov's and modern engines' favored Sicilian setups. Frequently reached via Najdorf or Taimanov move orders.
Existing standalone lesson (id smith-morra). Objectively close to equal with correct defense, but a favorite practical club-level weapon for its concrete, durable compensation on the open c/d-files.
Once considered dubious (weakens d5 permanently), rehabilitated by Sveshnikov and now one of the most respected and heavily analyzed Black systems at the top level.
Highly flexible move order that keeps options open between Scheveningen-, Kan-, and Hedgehog-type structures; a longtime favorite of positional grandmasters.

A real 19th/early-20th-century try with occasional modern club use, but objectively dubious against accurate defense (2...cxb4 followed by ...d5 is comfortable for Black). Kept as historical rather than excluded because it has genuine (if dated) theoretical status and name recognition.

Famous chiefly for Tony Miles's 1980 win over Anatoly Karpov playing it; genuine historical/cultural value as a surprise weapon but no serious independent body of theory — catalogued as historical rather than a mainstream defense.

Named for Dutch player Ad van Geet, with Theodore 'Ted' Dunst credited independently in American usage for the same first move. Real if rare tournament practice, valued mainly as a way to sidestep opponents' preparation rather than for independent theoretical content — tiered historical rather than specialized because serious modern practice is thin even at club level.

structures: asymmetrical material imbalance (White wins exchange, Black gets attack)
entries.notes: Named by Tim Harding (1976) for its 'bloodthirsty' forcing character; both sides' moves are close to forced for a long stretch, making it one of the most concretely-memorized lines in the whole 1.e4 e5 tree despite arising from a fairly rare parent move order (3.Bc4).

themes: King's Gambit-style attack with the knight already on c3
structures: White kingside pawn majority after trades
entries.notes: Delivers King's Gambit-style aggression but with Nc3 already developed, so Black cannot meet it with ...d5 Falkbeer-style counters as effectively. Distinct enough in move-order consequence to stand apart from the parent Vienna Game lesson.

structures: e4/f4 pawn duo in gambit lines
entries.notes: Develops the queen's knight before committing the f-pawn, keeping King's Gambit-style attacking options in reserve while avoiding some sharp KGA theory.

entries.moves: 1.Nf3 d5 2.g3 Nf6 3.Bg2 c5 4.O-O Nc6 5.d3 e5 6.Nbd2 Be7 7.e4
entries.notes: A White 'system' opening playable against nearly any Black defense (French, Caro-Kann, Sicilian, or 1...d5 setups) — most commonly reached via 1.Nf3/2.g3 (Réti move order, ECO A07-A08) but equally often via 1.e4 e6/e5/c5 2.d3 followed by g3 (adjacent to ECO C00/C20/B00). Catalogued once under its primary Réti-family classification; the 1.e4 route is noted as a transposition rather than duplicated as a separate entry.

The main practical try to hold the extra pawn is transient — White regains it in essentially all main lines — so this is a well-known branch rather than an independent battleground; taught inside the Réti Opening lesson.

motifs: c4/Bg2 battery on the long diagonal
entries.notes: Historically significant as the archetypal hypermodern opening (Réti's brilliancy over Capablanca, New York 1924); real modern practice at every level and a genuinely distinct hypermodern strategy from 1.d4/1.e4 openings — clears the standalone bar easily.

Umbrella/navigation entry for the many systems reachable from 1.Nf3 without an immediate central commitment; named for Johannes Zukertort more as ECO/database convention than as one coherent strategic identity. Houses the Réti Opening and King's Indian Attack as children for browsing — most independent theory and teaching content lives in those children, not here. Judgment call: included at the orchestrator's request for navigation, tiered specialized (not major) because its own independent content is thin.
